2027-05-29.title: Second Saturday of the Apostles
2027-05-29.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Sharing in the Body of Christ
2027-05-29.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. In the Latin calendar today is the optional memorial of St Paul VI, pope.
2027-05-29.verse: Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
theo: All week the readings have followed the sixth chapter of John; today, at the end of the week of the Body and Blood of Christ, we go back to its beginning, the sign that opened the whole discourse. A large crowd follows Jesus to the far side of the Sea of Galilee, and John notes that “the Passover, the festival of the Jews, was near.” The feeding is a Passover sign, pointing to the new Passover of the Last Supper. Jesus asks Philip, “Where are we to buy bread for these people to eat?” He asks it, John says, to test him, “for he himself knew what he was going to do.” Philip does the arithmetic: “Six months’ wages would not buy enough bread for each of them to get a little.” Andrew finds a boy: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are they among so many people?” Barley loaves were the bread of the poor. The boy gives what he has, and it is not enough, and Jesus does not ask for more. He takes it, gives thanks and distributes it, and some five thousand eat “as much as they wanted.” The words are the words of the Eucharist: he took the loaves, gave thanks, and distributed them. Every Holy Qurbana begins with our small offering, bread and wine and the gifts of the faithful, and the Lord does with it far more than we could imagine.

Two details are easy to miss. First: “When they were satisfied, he told his disciples, ‘Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost.’ So they gathered them up, and … they filled twelve baskets.” The Lord who gives in abundance does not waste. The twelve baskets, one for each apostle, are carried by the Twelve; they will feed the twelve tribes of a new Israel with what the Lord has blessed. And the words “so that nothing may be lost” echo what Jesus says later in the chapter about people: “that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me” (John 6:39). Second: when the crowd wants to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdraws to the mountain alone. He will not be a king who wins votes with bread. His kingship will be revealed on the Cross, and the bread he will give is his own flesh.

Paul draws the conclusion for a Church living among many altars. Corinth was full of temples, and meat sacrificed to idols was sold in the market and served at banquets. Paul writes: “Therefore, my dear friends, flee from the worship of idols.” Then he gives the reason: “The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.” The word translated sharing is koinonia, communion. Holy Communion is not a private devotion between me and Jesus; it makes us one body. That is why Paul says: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons.” He is not scorning the neighbours of the Corinthians; he is warning Christians against a divided heart. Our idols today are rarely made of stone or metal. They are money and success, the craving for approval, trust in charms and lucky days in place of trust in God. Whoever has eaten the one bread cannot give the heart to them. And whoever has eaten the one bread cannot ignore the hungry: the bread we break at the altar sends us to break our bread with the poor, and to gather up the fragments, so that nothing and no one is lost.
outline: Ask: what is my five loaves and two fish, and have I given it?
The boy's small gift, and the Lord who takes, gives thanks and distributes.
Point 2 · So that nothing may be lost
Twelve baskets, and the king who withdraws to the mountain.
Communion that makes us one, and the divided heart.
“We who are many are one body.”
live: Offer the Lord one small, concrete gift this week: an hour, a talent, a sum of money for someone in need.
Waste no food at home this week; share what is left over with someone who needs it.
fathers: The Lord who multiplied the five loaves is the same who every year multiplies a few seeds into whole harvests. Because that wonder happens every day, we have stopped marvelling at it; so he did on the mountain in an hour what he does in the fields in a year, that we might wake up and praise the Creator.

You honour the Body of Christ at the altar with silk vestments; do not despise him when he is naked in the poor. What use is it to load his table with golden cups if he himself is dying of hunger? First feed the hungry, then adorn the altar with what remains.
magis: The miracles of the multiplication of the loaves, when the Lord said the blessing, broke and distributed the loaves through his disciples to feed the multitude, prefigure the superabundance of this unique bread of his Eucharist.
The unity of the Mystical Body: the Eucharist makes the Church. Those who receive the Eucharist are united more closely to Christ, and Christ unites them to all the faithful in one body.
The Eucharist commits us to the poor. To receive in truth the Body and Blood of Christ given up for us, we must recognise Christ in the poorest, his brethren.
saints: Latin calendar: St Paul VI (1897–1978), pope from 1963 to 1978, who brought the Second Vatican Council to its close. In December 1964 he came to Bombay for the International Eucharistic Congress, the first pope to visit India. On Saturdays, and in this last week of May, we also turn to the Mother of God.

26–31 May: second and third weeks of the Season of the Apostles. Wed 26: in the Latin calendar, St Philip Neri. Thu 27: the Feast of the Body and Blood of Christ (the Latin Church in India keeps Corpus Christi on Sunday 30 May). Sat 29: in the Latin calendar, St Paul VI. Sun 30: Third Sunday of the Apostles. Mon 31: the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which closes the month of Mary. The Sacred Heart of Jesus falls on Friday 4 June.
2027-05-29.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you took the boy's five barley loaves, gave thanks and fed the multitude, and you told your disciples to gather the fragments so that nothing might be lost. Take the little we have and make it enough for others. You are the one bread that makes us one body: keep our hearts undivided, turned away from every idol, and open to the hungry. Through the prayers of Mary, your Mother, who gave you flesh, make us faithful to the table of the Lord. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the offertory of the Holy Qurbana the Church brings bread and wine, our five loaves and two fish. The Lord takes them, gives thanks and makes them his Body and Blood, the one bread that makes us one body.

quick: A boy gives five barley loaves and two fish; Jesus gives thanks and feeds five thousand.
Gather up the fragments so that nothing may be lost: twelve baskets are left over; Jesus refuses to be made a king of bread.
Paul: the cup of blessing and the bread we break are a sharing in the blood and body of Christ; one bread, one body.
2027-05-29.action: Waste no food this week, and share what is left over with someone in need.
2027-05-29.question: What small gift am I holding back because I think it is not enough?

family.explain: Thousands of hungry people followed Jesus. A boy had five small loaves and two fish, and he gave them to Jesus. Jesus thanked God, and everyone ate until they were full! Then Jesus said, “Gather up what is left over, so that nothing is wasted,” and there were twelve baskets full. Jesus can do great things with the little we give him.
family.intention: We pray for families who do not have enough to eat today.
family.ask: Ask: “What can each of us give to Jesus this week, even if it seems small?”

illus: In a parish near Thrissur the youth group noticed how much food was thrown away after big weddings and feasts. They made an arrangement with three auditoriums: when a function ended, the manager would call them. Within an hour, a group of young people with clean containers would collect the untouched food and take it to an old-age home, a hostel for migrant workers and two families in the parish who were struggling. The first time they went, one boy grumbled that it was beneath him to carry leftovers. On the way back he said quietly, ‘Now I understand why Jesus told the disciples to gather up the fragments.’ The group named their work ‘Twelve Baskets’.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you fed the hungry crowd with five barley loaves. Take the little we bring tonight and bless it, and make us one body in you. Amen.
share: There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish (John 6:9). What small gift do I have to offer?
Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost (John 6:12). What or whom am I wasting or neglecting?
The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ? (1 Corinthians 10:16). How does Communion make me one with others?
Flee from the worship of idols (1 Corinthians 10:14). What has taken God's place in my heart?
pm.resp: Lord, bread of life, make us one.
interc: For the Church, that the one bread may make her one body, healed of every division.
For the hungry and the poor, that those who share the Eucharist may share their bread.
For families who waste and families who want, that God may teach us to gather the fragments.
For those who trust in charms and lucky days instead of God, that they may find peace in the Lord.
Through the intercession of the Mother of God, for all who have prayed the devotions of the month of May.
pm.close: Father, your Son took the little that was offered and fed a multitude. Bless our small gifts, keep our hearts from idols, and make us who share the one bread one body in Christ, caring for the least of our brothers and sisters. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, a huge crowd followed Jesus, and there was nothing to eat. Philip counted the cost: six months' wages would not be enough. Andrew found a boy with five barley loaves and two fish, and said, “But what are they among so many people?” (John 6:9).

The boy gave what he had. It was not enough. But Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks and distributed them, and five thousand ate as much as they wanted. Those are the words of the Holy Qurbana: he took, gave thanks, and gave. Never think your gift is too small for God.

Then Jesus said, “Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost” (John 6:12). Twelve baskets were filled. The Lord gives in abundance, but nothing is wasted, and no one is to be lost. Let us waste no food, and gather up the ones the world forgets.

Saint Paul says: the bread that we break is a sharing in the body of Christ; because there is one bread, we who are many are one body (1 Corinthians 10:16–17). Communion makes us one. So we cannot give our hearts to idols, to money, success or charms, and we cannot forget the hungry.
This is the last Saturday of the month of Mary. She gave the Lord her whole self, and he took flesh from her. Let us give him our five loaves today, and let him make them bread for many. Amen.
kids: Children, a boy gave Jesus his lunch: five small loaves and two fish. Jesus thanked God and fed five thousand people! And there were twelve baskets left over. Give Jesus what you have, even if it is small, and see what he can do with it!
